result.target_summary: The Corporate Transparency Act (CTA), enacted in 2021 as part of the AMLA, established beneficial ownership information reporting requirements implemented by a FinCEN rule effective in 2024. Domestic companies formed before 2024 must file initial reports by January 1, 2025 (later announced as March 21, 2025), while those formed in or after 2024 must file within 90 or 30 days of formation, subject to exemptions.

target_year_over_year_context.explanation: This is a many-to-many split. D156 (2023) covers the AMLA broadly: reforming/modernizing BSA, risk-based approach, Treasury priorities, enforcement expansion, whistleblower protections, and FinCEN priorities. In 2024, this broad AMLA topic is split into multiple disclosures: D150 covers the consolidated BSA/AMLA framework; D151 covers the AMLA impact depending on rulemaking and FinCEN priorities; D152 covers the Corporate Transparency Act (enacted as part of AMLA); D153 covers specific proposed/adopted rules for investment advisers under AMLA/BSA. Each 2024 disclosure addresses a specific sub-topic introduced or contained within D156. We provide separate rows for the logical links: D156->D151 (AMLA impact/priorities), D156->D152 (AMLA/CTA), D156->D153 (AMLA/Investment Adviser rules), and D156->D150 (AMLA/BSA framework). Note: D150 is also linked from D155. This is allowed as separate rows.

current_disclosures.section: Regulation > Anti-Money Laundering and Anti-Bribery Rules and Regulations
current_disclosures.summary: The U.S. Bank Secrecy Act (BSA), as amended by the USA PATRIOT Act and the Anti-Money Laundering Act of 2020 (AMLA), establishes anti-money laundering and financial transparency laws requiring client identification, transaction monitoring, and suspicious activity reporting. The AMLA comprehensively reformed these laws by codifying a risk-based compliance approach, expanding enforcement authorities and sanctions, and requiring Treasury to set priorities and test standards.

current_disclosures.section: Regulation > Anti-Money Laundering and Anti-Bribery Rules and Regulations
current_disclosures.summary: The impact of the AMLA depends on additional rulemakings and implementation guidance, though the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) has already issued required anti-money laundering and countering the financing of terrorism priorities. These priorities include corruption, cybercrime, terrorist financing, fraud, transnational crime, drug trafficking, human trafficking, and proliferation financing.

current_disclosures.section: Regulation > Anti-Money Laundering and Anti-Bribery Rules and Regulations
current_disclosures.summary: In 2024, FinCEN and the SEC proposed rules requiring investment advisers to implement procedures to identify and verify customer identities, and FinCEN proposed amendments to BSA program requirements including periodic risk assessments. Additionally, FinCEN adopted a rule effective January 1, 2026, including certain investment advisers in the definition of 'financial institutions' under BSA rules, prescribing minimum AML/CFT program standards and suspicious activity reporting obligations.

comparisons.peer_topic: Disclosure controls and procedures definition and purpose
comparisons.peer_summary: Citi's disclosure controls and procedures are designed to ensure information required under the Securities Exchange Act is recorded, processed, and reported within SEC time periods, including accumulation and communication to the CEO and CFO for timely decisions.
comparisons.comparison: Citi’s disclosure focuses on internal disclosure controls and procedures to ensure timely reporting under the Securities Exchange Act of 1934, which differs from Goldman Sachs’ disclosure of external beneficial ownership reporting mandates imposed by FinCEN under the Corporate Transparency Act. Both relate to regulatory reporting compliance, but Citi’s is an internal control mechanism for general SEC filings, whereas GS’s is a specific new external filing requirement for corporate ownership data.

sentences.text: The Corporate Transparency Act (CTA) was enacted in 2021 as part of the AMLA and designed to establish beneficial ownership information reporting requirements for certain types of entities, and in 2024, FinCEN's rule implementing the reporting requirements of the CTA became effective.

Citi's disclosure controls and procedures are designed to ensure that information required to be disclosed under the Securities Exchange Act of 1934, as amended, is recorded, processed, summarized and reported within the time periods specified in the SEC's rules and forms, including without limitation that information required to be disclosed by Citi in its SEC filings is accumulated and communicated to management, including the Chief Executive Officer (CEO) and Chief Financial Officer (CFO), as appropriate, to allow for timely decisions regarding required disclosure.

comparisons.peer_summary: The Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive (CSRD) will replace and expand EU ESG reporting requirements starting in fiscal year 2024, with implementation delays in some member states, while the Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive (CSDDD) enacted in July 2024 mandates due diligence obligations for human rights and environmental impacts starting in 2027, impacting the Firm's EU and non-EU entities.
comparisons.comparison: JPMorgan Chase’s disclosure addresses EU sustainability reporting directives (CSRD/CSDDD) which expand ESG disclosure requirements, whereas Goldman Sachs discloses U.S. beneficial ownership reporting requirements under the CTA. Both represent significant new regulatory reporting mandates affecting large financial institutions, but they diverge in geographic scope (EU vs. U.S.) and subject matter (ESG vs. ownership transparency).

comparisons.peer_topic: Broker-dealer, CTA/CPO status, and Volcker Rule restrictions
comparisons.peer_summary: Certain subsidiaries are U.S. registered broker-dealers acting as distributors or placement agents, while affiliates serve as commodity trading advisors/operators under CFTC rules or exemptions, with activities also subject to Volcker Rule restrictions on covered funds.
comparisons.comparison: Morgan Stanley’s disclosure highlights Volcker Rule restrictions on investments in covered funds, which is a restriction on activity, whereas Goldman Sachs’ disclosure concerns mandatory reporting of beneficial ownership information under the CTA. Both are regulatory compliance topics under U.S. financial laws, but they differ fundamentally in nature: one prohibits/limits specific financial activities, while the other requires data disclosure regarding corporate structure.
